# Reflection — ExploreQuest

> **Note:** This feedback is AI-generated and experimental. It's meant to surface useful observations, not to grade you. Take what resonates, ignore what doesn't. Your own sense of what you learned matters more than anything here.

## Scope & Idea Clarity

**What went well:** The pivot decision itself was sharp. After completing a full build of the original StudyQuest, the learner decided to restart as a pure exploration game — and the scope doc reflects that cleanly. Specific gameplay loop, specific tech stack, and a "What's NOT in scope" list that's actually meaningful (no AI, no database, no procedural generation). Writing explicit cut lists is not obvious for a first-timer; most people list what they want but not what they won't build.

**What to try next time:** The target user is implicit. The scope describes the mechanic well but doesn't say who the game is for or why they'd play it. Even one line — "a 5-minute pick-up-and-play game for someone who wants a quick win" — would sharpen every downstream decision about difficulty, length, and feel.

## Requirements Thinking

**What went well:** The acceptance criteria in the PRD are testable and specific. "Boss touching player deals 1 HP damage to the player (once per second max)" is a real acceptance criterion — you can actually verify it. Concrete numbers appear throughout: 60px attack range, 2-second float label fade, 60-frame attack cooldown. That specificity made the build go smoothly and left no ambiguity for the code to fill in.

**What to try next time:** The PRD has no edge cases for boss fight entry or inventory access. What happens if the player presses E before collecting all 3 items? What about opening inventory during the boss fight? These weren't disasters in practice, but one round of "what's the weird thing a player might do?" during PRD review is a habit worth building. Think through the failure modes before you build, not after.

## Technical Decisions

**What went well:** The architecture decision to keep all game logic in a single `game.js` with a clean state machine (`'start' | 'game' | 'boss' | 'win' | 'lose'`) was the right call for a hackathon scope. Simple, readable, and traceable. The spec's rendering order (clear → sky → tiles → chests → boss → player → labels → HUD) maps directly to the code's draw sequence — that kind of spec-to-code traceability is hard to achieve and the build landed it.

**What to try next time:** The spec describes a minimal map; the actual code has 8 platform groups, 4 high platforms, parallax mountains, clouds, trees, and underground crystals — none of which are in the spec. That's not bad (the game looks better for it), but it means the spec stopped being the source of truth mid-build. When you expand the design during a build, update the spec or note the additions in process notes. A spec is most useful when it reflects what was actually built.

## Plan vs. Reality

**What went well:** All 6 code checklist items are complete, and the code confirms it — the full loop from project setup through boss fight to win/lose screens is there. For an autonomous build of a browser game from scratch in one session, that's a clean result. The checkpoint structure (verify exploration before building boss fight) was a smart sequencing call.

**What to try next time:** The code has features the checklist never planned: Web Audio music with two tracks, a start screen, mouse-click attack, player facing direction, boss hit flash, attack animation state. These are genuine improvements — but item 7 (Devpost submission) is unchecked. The pattern is scope creep on polish, incomplete on the final deliverable. Next time: finish the checklist first, then add extras. A submitted project beats a polished unsubmitted one every time.

## How You Worked

**What went well:** The pivot is the standout moment. Completing a full 8-item build and then deciding to restart as a different project because it better fit what you actually wanted — that's an active, opinionated decision. You didn't accept the first version. That kind of ownership is exactly the difference between using an AI tool and being driven by one.

**What to try next time:** The rebuild was done in a single autonomous session with no comprehension checks. That works for shipping fast, but on a longer project it can leave you holding code you don't fully understand — like the Web Audio system or the parallax rendering added beyond the spec. Try stepping through one or two of the more complex pieces yourself next time. Ask "how does this work?" before moving on. You'll debug faster and extend the code more confidently.

## Your Goals

You came in with three goals: learn the full procedure of finishing a project, get real experience using AI agents, and build hackathon experience.

On the first — you went through scope, PRD, spec, checklist, and build twice. You articulated it yourself: "a project doesn't have to be too big, just make it run first, then iterate." That's not just a lesson learned — that's a working mental model you can take into the next project.

On the second — you used Claude to build a working browser game from scratch and felt the real tension of AI-assisted development firsthand. The speed surprised you ("few minutes vs. few days"), but you also noticed it built what *you* designed. That instinct — the AI is fast, but the judgment is yours — is the right one to hold onto.

On the third — ExploreQuest is a real, playable, visually complete game. The one gap: item 7 (Devpost submission) is unchecked. If you want hackathon experience, submitting is part of it.

## Reflection

When asked what surprised them most, the learner said: "I was surprised that there are so many ideas coming through my mind, and I don't know what should I do at the beginning. And also, AI coding is way too fast — just only a few minutes, build up a project that I would take a few hours or even days to finish."

Both surprises point at real things. The flood of ideas is exactly why the scoping step exists — not to limit you, but to give all those ideas a place to land so you can choose deliberately. The speed of the build is real, but the speed is the tool; the judgment was yours. The scope, the PRD, the spec — that was you.
